title: Hurry toward good (116–118)
hookLine: make haste to do good; a mind slow in doing good delights in evil

lines: A CHAPTER THAT OPENS WITH SPEED.
cards: A friend posts that she's having a rough week, and the thought comes: I should text her. Then the kettle boils, an email lands, and suddenly it's Thursday.
Or a neighbor is wrestling a heavy bin down the driveway, and the thought is: next time I'll help. The good impulse was real. It just wasn't fast.
Chapter nine of the Dhammapada is called evil, and a chapter with that name could open with villains. It doesn't. It opens with a word about speed.

teach.b: Verse one sixteen, in Max Müller's 1881 translation: "If a man would hasten towards the good, he should keep his thought away from evil; if a man does what is good slothfully, his mind delights in evil."
The verse assumes the mind is never empty. If good dawdles, something else moves into the space.

And the word Müller translates as evil, pāpa in Pali, is wider than wickedness: anything harmful or unskillful, the small unkindness as much as the crime. The old commentary tells a story behind this verse.
A poor brahmin and his wife owned a single outer cloth between them, so only one of them could go out at a time. One night, listening to the Buddha teach, he wanted to offer that cloth.
In the first watch of the night he hesitated: what would they wear? In the second watch, the same. In the third, he finally gave it, and cried out, I have won!
The commentary says the gift was good, and that if he'd given it in the first watch, it would have borne even more fruit. The next two verses turn from speed to repetition.
Verse one seventeen: "If a man commits a sin, let him not do it again; let him not delight in sin: pain is the outcome of evil."
And verse one eighteen: "If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good."
Hurry, then repeat. That's how a habit gets built, in either direction.

how: Buddhist teaching treats an impulse to give or help as something to act on promptly, and teachers tell the commentary's story of the brahmin with one cloth when they explain this verse.

o: rush through good deeds to get them done
do good mainly to earn a quick reward
act on a good impulse quickly, before it fades

games.q: match each verse to what it says.
p: a harm done: don't do it again
a good done: do it again

s: in this chapter, evil only means great wickedness
the Pali word pāpa covers any harmful or unskillful act, the small ones too.
in the commentary's story, the brahmin gave his cloth in the first watch of the night
he hesitated through two watches and gave it in the third.
verse 118 says to repeat a good deed and delight in it
"let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good."

games.q: you're the brahmin who shares one cloth with his wife. the Buddha is teaching, and you want to offer it. it's the first watch of the night. what do you do?
o: wait, and think it over until later.
keep it; it's all you have.
games.why: he waited through two watches and gave it in the third. the commentary says the gift was good, and an earlier one would have borne more fruit.

practice: Ask quietly: what's one good thing I've been meaning to do? A text, a thank-you, returning something borrowed, a small apology.
Notice the small voice that says later; you don't have to argue with it, just see it and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Hurry toward good. Verse one sixteen: make haste toward the good, because a mind that dawdles over good drifts toward harm.

orig.note: Pali: good, and also lovely or beautiful — the good that verse 116 says to hurry toward.

carryVoice: Your line: hurry toward the good. The brahmin got there in the third watch. Day one hundred eighty-one.
